question:
A 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of swelling around his eyes for 4 days. The swelling is most severe in the morning and milder by bedtime. Ten days ago, he had a sore throat that resolved spontaneously. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 103/min, and blood pressure is 88/52 mm Hg. Examination shows 3+ pitting edema of the lower extremities and periorbital edema. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 15.3 g/dL
Leukocyte count 10,500/mm3
Platelet count 480,000/mm3
Serum
Urea nitrogen 36 mg/dL
Glucose 67 mg/dL
Creatinine 0.8 mg/dL
Albumin 2.6 mg/dL
Urine
Blood negative
Glucose negative
Protein 4+
RBC none
WBC 0–1/hpf
Fatty casts numerous
Protein/creatinine ratio 6.8 (N ≤0.2)
Serum complement concentrations are within the reference ranges. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?"?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Recent sore throat" -> "possible post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis" -> "check Anti-streptolysin O levels" -> 85%
CHAIN: "Periorbital and lower extremity edema" -> "nephrotic syndrome" -> "Prednisone therapy for inflammation and immune modulation" -> 80%
CHAIN: "Low serum albumin" -> "increased renal loss of proteins" -> "nephrotic syndrome" -> "Prednisone therapy to reduce proteinuria and inflammation" -> 82%
CHAIN: "Proteinuria with protein/creatinine ratio 6.8" -> "significant kidney involvement" -> "Prednisone therapy to reduce kidney inflammation" -> 78%
CHAIN: "Numerous fatty casts in urine" -> "nephrotic syndrome" -> "Prednisone therapy to manage symptoms and prevent complications" -> 75%
CHAIN: "Recent sore throat followed by swelling and proteinuria" -> "post-infectious glomerulonephritis" -> "Prednisone therapy to control immune response" -> 70%
analysis: The clinical presentation and laboratory findings suggest the child has nephrotic syndrome, characterized by proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and edema. The history of a recent sore throat followed by these symptoms raises the possibility of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis; however, the normal complement levels and absence of hematuria make this less likely. The presence of numerous fatty casts and significant proteinuria with a normal complement profile is more suggestive of minimal change disease, a common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children. Prednisone is the first-line treatment for minimal change disease, as it is often responsive to corticosteroids, leading to a reduction in proteinuria and resolution of edema.
